title: Where do swear words come from?

entries.note: Not an acronym but an old Germanic word, possibly from a root meaning to hit, like [[same-root?:pugnus]], or from Middle English [[from?:fiken]], to fidget; cognate with [[same-root:ficken]].

entries.term: fornication under consent of the king
entries.note: A bogus acronym origin for [[see:fuck]], dismissed as nonsense because the word is far older than any acronym.
Another false acronym for [[see:fuck]]; at the time, words like [[see:knowledge]] were spelled differently, so the letters would not match.
Acronyms are a relatively recent, industrial-era kind of wordplay, which is why acronym explanations for old words like [[see:fuck]] fail.
Like [[see:house]], it comes from a word simply meaning house, but Norman associations made it seem fancier, showing why Germanic words seem more basic or vulgar.
The plain Germanic counterpart of [[see:mansion]], given as an example of how Norman influence made Anglo-Saxon words seem humbler.
Once spelled with a C, so it could not supply the K in the false acronym [[see:for unlawful carnal knowledge]].
Latin for fist, possibly linked to [[same-root?:fuck]] through a root meaning to hit; it gave [[gave:pugnacious]] and [[gave:pugilist]].
Means a bit punchy; from Latin [[from:pugnus]], which may share a root with [[same-root?:fuck]].
A boxer, from Latin [[from:pugnus]]; mentioned to back up the theory that [[see:fuck]] comes from a root meaning to hit.
The German word for the act, which would connect to [[same-root:fuck]] if fuck comes from a Germanic source describing rapid movement.
An Old English word meaning to move lightly over or sweep, also used as a euphemism for sex, supporting the rapid-movement theory of [[see:fuck]].
A Middle English name that probably meant John the Restless or fidgety, evidence that [[see:fuck]] once had a benign meaning.
A 13th-century personal name, cited as evidence that [[see:fuck]] was once relatively benign.
A medieval surname that makes Rob blush, another early name containing [[see:fuck]].
The original name of a place in Bristol; unlike most rude place names, which were softened, it was dropped altogether. Evidence of [[see:fuck]]'s former mildness.
An old name for the kestrel, probably referring to it striking the wind or moving rapidly; related dialect names include [[see:windsucker]] and [[see:windcuffer]].
A modern dialect word for the kestrel, probably derived from [[from?:windfucker]].
Another dialect word for the kestrel, probably derived from [[from?:windfucker]].
The process of a word becoming more profane or negative over time, discussed before and illustrated here by [[see:fuck]]; the opposite of [[see:amelioration]].
A word becoming gentler over time, as [[see:fuck]] has partly done through overuse; the opposite of [[see:pejoration]].
A comedian whose routine traced [[see:fuck]] to a Middle English word meaning to press hard; his slightly wrong facts came from [[see:Joseph T. Shipley]].
The etymologist [[see:George Carlin]] relied on; lexicographers have since picked parts of his work apart, which explains Carlin's errors.

entries.term: seven words you can never say on television
entries.note: [[see:George Carlin]]'s 1972 routine, also called the filthy words routine, listing words emblematic of censorship; it led to the [[see:FCC v. Pacifica Foundation]] case.
One of the words on [[see:seven words you can never say on television]].
US TV stations bleep it even though they let [[see:ass]] through.
The BBC and Ofcom treat it as more severe than plain [[see:fuck]], reflecting how insulting mothers is a common swearing trope worldwide; it is among Ofcom's strongest words.
Taking the Lord's name in vain is considered less severe in Britain than in the United States.
Rated mild on Ofcom's survey-based list of swear words.

Rated mild by Ofcom; sod refers to Sodom and Gomorrah through [[from:sodomite]].
Someone who behaves the way people did in Sodom; the source of [[gave:sod off]].
Rated medium by Ofcom, oddly above [[see:bugger]]; named because testicles look like balls, and the base of [[gave:bollocks]].
Rated medium on Ofcom's list of swear words.
Rated strong by Ofcom, though Jess sees it as a silly rude word and sometimes a factual term.
Rated strong on Ofcom's list, which the hosts find surprising.
Rated strong on Ofcom's list, to the hosts' amusement.
Rated strong by Ofcom; a Romany or Traveller word.

Sounds antiquated to Rob as a word for a swear word; like swearing and cursing, it comes from solemnly swearing by a deity.
Comes from judicial or solemn swearing by a deity; [[see:John Ruskin]] defined it as invoking a spirit's witness, unlike a [[see:curse]].
Rob sees it as an Americanism for swear word; it can mean invoking gods to harm others, and [[see:John Ruskin]] distinguished it from [[see:swear]].
Raised as possibly a separate type of swear word, alongside [[see:oath]], [[see:swear]] and [[see:curse]].
Saying something that sounds like a swear word in order to avoid saying the swear word itself.
Victorian thinker who distinguished [[see:swear]] from [[see:curse]] and called people who mixed them up ill-educated and ill-tempered.
Always consists of words, whereas [[see:obscenity]] can be other kinds of art.
Unlike [[see:profanity]], it is not limited to words; it can be other kinds of art, such as [[see:Fanny Hill]].
A 1748 novel, Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure, among the first novel-length English pornography, now public domain; its heroine gave us [[gave:fanny]].
From [[from:Fanny Hill]]; in Britain a fairly rude word for female genitals, in the US a milder word for the backside, and also a nickname for Frances.
Penguin won the court case over publishing it in the 1960s, ending enforcement of British obscenity laws and letting swear words into dictionaries.
Landmark case over a radio broadcast of [[see:seven words you can never say on television]], which found it indecent but not obscene, so it could air outside safe-harbor hours.
Originally a filler word like oh in verse, used to pad the metre; its link with swearing came from [[see:expletive deleted]]. Rob and Jess stress different syllables.
Used in the Watergate tape transcripts in place of Nixon's swearing; it became a meme and tied [[see:expletive]] to swearing.
Old English, perhaps from Latin [[from?:cunnus]] or [[from?:cuneus]], wedge, or a root meaning hollow, woman or slit; harsher toward women in America, used more freely in Australia.
Originally meaning clever or skilful, later cute; it was also an old word for the vagina, punned on with [[see:cunt]] by Chaucer.
A British etymology TV show presented by Victoria Coren Mitchell, on which [[see:Germaine Greer]] praised the word [[see:cunt]].
An Australian feminist, a big deal in Britain, who praised [[see:cunt]] on [[see:Balderdash and Piffle]] as better than words like [[see:pudenda]].
A word for the genitals that Rob considers the worst because of its unpleasant literal meaning.
Means a sword sheath, framing the body part by its use to men, as discussed in a past episode.
A street name for places where sex workers were found, recorded in Oxford and elsewhere; York's [[see:Grape Lane]] may once have had it.
A former Lincolnshire place name, cited as evidence that [[see:cunt]] was once used matter-of-factly.
A Kent place name containing [[see:cunt]]; it is now called Shinglewell.
A street in York thought to have once been a [[see:Gropecunt Lane]].
A personal name recorded in 1066, one of several medieval names containing [[see:cunt]].

A deep-sea worm named because it looks like a pig's bottom, though Jess thinks it looks like something ruder.
A mild insult, short for the rhyming slang [[from:Berkeley Hunt]], so it evokes [[see:cunt]].
Contains Latin [[from:cunnus]], a possible source of [[same-root?:cunt]].
A French swear word for an idiot that ultimately shares the meaning of [[same-root:cunt]].
Hamlet's line after offering to lay his head in Ophelia's lap, a Shakespearean pun on [[see:cunt]].
Evokes [[see:piss]] by its first letter, the same way [[see:effing]] evokes [[see:fuck]].
Evokes [[see:fuck]] by its first letter, just as [[see:pee]] evokes [[see:piss]].
Imitative of the sound of urinating; Rob was raised to see it as a swear word, though it is fairly mild.
Means drunk in Britain, where calling yourself a bit pissed is acceptable, and angry in America.
Telling someone to piss off would be harsh, unlike describing yourself as [[see:pissed]].
Francis Grose's euphemism for [[see:cunt]] in his Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue, defined as a woman's commodity and a nasty word for a nasty thing.
Also Miss Brown, one of Grose's synonyms for the [[see:monosyllable]].
One of Grose's synonyms for the [[see:monosyllable]], among many rabbit jokes.
Meant both a rabbit and female genitals, which inspired the rabbit-themed synonyms for the [[see:monosyllable]].
A synonym for the [[see:monosyllable]], so called because it was where Adam made his first entry.
One of Grose's synonyms for the [[see:monosyllable]].

A Farmer and Henley synonym for the [[see:monosyllable]], because that's where you play; Jess's new favourite.
Pronounced differently by Rob and Jess; perhaps from twixt your legs, or a filler sound in songs like twitty twatty, as with [[see:dildo]] and [[see:nonny]].
Began as a filler sound in songs, like tra-la-la; [[see:The Choice of Valentines]] first used it for a sex toy in 1592.
A slang word for a vagina that, like [[see:dildo]], came from a filler sound in songs.
A filthy 1592 poem, also called the Merry Ballad of Nashe His Dildo, about a man and a sex worker; it cemented [[see:dildo]] as a sex toy.
A fairly mild insult; the nickname for Richard, used as an everyman name like Jack in [[see:Tom, Dick and Harry]], then for the penis, like [[see:Johnson]].
An old word for the periwinkle, showing [[see:dick]] used as a generic name.
An old name for a will-o'-the-wisp, another use of [[see:dick]] as a generic name.
Mentioned jokingly as another harmless use of [[see:dick]].
An old term for a jackass, in which [[see:dick]] works like Jack as an everyman name.
The best example of [[see:dick]] used as an everyman name.
Like [[see:dick]], a man's name used for the penis, as if it were your little fellow.
Originally a rooster; early penis uses were metaphorical or in [[from:pillicock]]; taps called cocks, like [[see:stopcock]], were rooster-shaped, not phallic.
The early compound form behind the penis sense of [[gave:cock]], with pill meaning skin: literally skin rooster.
A tap called a [[see:cock]] because early spouts were shaped like roosters, crest and all.
From [[from:balls]] plus the diminutive [[see:-ock]], meaning small balls; talking bollocks means talking rubbish, and Americans only use it to sound British.
An old diminutive suffix meaning little, found in [[see:bollocks]], [[see:bullock]] and [[see:buttock]].
Another word with the diminutive [[see:-ock]].
The little bits that make up your butt, formed with the diminutive [[see:-ock]].
From Latin scrotum, purse, so it is literally a little purse for the testicles.
Ruder than breasts but rarely bleeped in the US; originally meant something small, or was a variant of [[see:teat]]; in Britain, a mild insult for a petty person.
The British spelling; Americans may prefer tidbit to avoid saying [[see:tit]], though the hosts doubt it, since Americans still say [[see:titmouse]].
A bird name Americans still use, which undermines the idea that they avoid [[see:tit]].
[[see:tit]] may be a variant of it; it's hard to tell which came first.
The character from the original series of The Office, given as the perfect example of a [[see:tit]]: not malevolent, just a tit.
Also used to call someone a fool, a parallel to the insult [[see:tit]].
The bird is named for its awkward walk; the hosts' favourite funny bird name after [[see:windfucker]].
Named as another funny bird name, alongside [[see:booby]].
The donkey sense came first and is widespread in Indo-European; the bottom sense comes from [[see:arse]], with the two conflated by the 1500s; related to [[same-root:asinine]].
From the Latin word for a donkey, so related to the donkey sense of [[same-root:ass]].
The old word for the rear end, used by Chaucer; poets rhymed it with class and pass from the 1500s, so it merged with [[see:ass]].
Full of [[see:ass]] puns, including Bottom's triple pun on donkey, buffoon and bottom, showing the bottom sense existed long before the 1860s.
Not an acronym like [[see:ship high in transit]] but from the Old English verb for pooping, from a root meaning to divide that also gave [[same-root:science]]; very versatile.
A silly false acronym for [[see:shit]], said to have been stamped on manure boxes; there is no record of it ever happening.
A gentler version of [[see:shit]] whose long I sound better reflects the Old English spelling.
A Lincolnshire place originally called Shitbrook; its SK shows Norse influence, as with [[see:shirt]] and [[see:skirt]].
The Old English form of a word that shares its origin with the Viking [[same-root:skirt]].
The Viking counterpart of [[same-root:shirt]], with SK where Old English had a SH sound.
A London street originally called Shitteborwelane, roughly meaning shit-borne lane, containing [[see:shit]].
A Warwickshire farm originally called Shitwell, another place name containing [[see:shit]].
Shares with [[same-root:shit]] a root meaning to divide, as science separates truth from fiction; also linked to [[same-root:decision]], [[same-root:scissors]] and [[same-root?:scatological]].

Very drunk; another expression built on [[see:shit]].
Used jokingly near the end of the episode as one more expression built on [[see:shit]].
